title: Prayer is relationship (CCC 2558–2565)
hookLine: prayer is the raising of mind and heart to God

lines: A TIRED TRAVELER ASKS FOR A DRINK.
cards: Samaria, about the sixth hour, John says: around noon. A woman comes to draw water at Jacob's well. A tired Jewish traveler sitting by it asks her for a drink.
She's startled; Jews and Samaritans, John notes, keep apart. Then he turns the whole conversation upside down: if you knew who was asking, you'd be the one asking him, and he'd give you living water.
Near the very start of its teaching on prayer, the Catechism comes right here, to this well. Not with a rule. With someone who's thirsty, asking someone else for a drink.

teach.b: Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "If thou didst know the gift of God, and who he is that saith to thee, Give me to drink; thou perhaps wouldst have asked of him, and he would have given thee living water."
The Catechism draws a line from it, following Augustine: God thirsts for us first, so that we might thirst for him. Prayer starts with God's desire.

teach.h: RAISING MIND AND HEART TO GOD.
teach.b: The Catechism gives a classic definition from the monk John Damascene: prayer is the raising of one's mind and heart to God. Not a technique. A lifting.
It adds Thérèse of Lisieux's version: prayer as a movement of the heart, a simple look toward heaven, a cry of gratitude and love in trouble and in joy.

teach.h: A GIFT, A COVENANT, A COMMUNION.
teach.b: The Catechism calls prayer a gift, a covenant and a communion: the living relationship of God's children with their Father, through Christ, in the Spirit. That's why prayer can be words, or silence, or tears, or a glance.
Friends don't always talk in full sentences.

teach.h: SURSUM CORDA: LIFT UP YOUR HEARTS.
teach.b: Right before the great prayer at the heart of the Mass, the priest says lift up your hearts; in Latin, sursum corda.
It echoes a line in Lamentations: "Let us lift up our hearts with our hands to the Lord in the heavens."
Over these last six weeks you've walked the Catechism: the desire for God, faith and reason, the Trinity, creation, the fall, the Incarnation, grace, the virtues, the Church, the last things.
Catholics could say all of it leads here: to a heart, lifted.

how: At every Mass the priest says lift up your hearts before the Eucharistic Prayer, and the people answer that they lift them up to the Lord; many Catholics also pray briefly through the day, in short prayers, silence, or the Liturgy of the Hours.

o: lift up your hearts, a call to raise them to God
a prayer for the hearts of the sick and dying
the Latin blessing the priest gives at the end

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.
p: raising of mind and heart to God

s: the Catechism says prayer starts with our effort
following Augustine, it says God thirsts for us first, so that we might thirst for him.
prayer, in Catholic teaching, can be silent
it's a living relationship: words, silence, tears, or a simple look.
sursum corda is said at every Mass
lift up your hearts, just before the Eucharistic Prayer.

games.q: you're the Samaritan woman. a tired Jewish traveler asks you for a drink at the well. what does he say next?
o: if you knew who was asking, you'd ask him, and he'd give you living water.
he asks you to leave the well.
games.why: the one who asks for a drink offers living water. the Catechism turns to this well near the start of its teaching on prayer.

practice: Notice what your heart is carrying right now, a worry, a thanks, a person, a tiredness, and hold it without sorting it. Then, on one breath, lift it, the way you'd lift a cup toward someone across a table.
If you pray, that lifting is a prayer you can let go to God; if you don't, lift it toward the light, and rest.

wordCard.voice: Sursum corda, the priest's call before the Eucharistic Prayer, lift up your hearts: prayer as a relationship, a heart raised to God. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: lift up your hearts, the priest's call just before the Eucharistic Prayer.

carryVoice: Your line: lift up your heart. Tomorrow, the last day of year one: the big lookout.
